o: Select storage for a real-world scenario.
r: Name the three main secondary-storage technologies.
Magnetic, optical and solid state.
Why can heavy virtual-memory use reduce performance?
Frequent transfers to/from slower secondary storage.
Which compression type should be used when the original program file must be restored exactly?
Lossless.
A handheld data logger is frequently dropped and must access files quickly. Recommend a storage technology and justify it against an HDD.
Solid-state storage: no moving parts makes it more shock-resistant, and access is generally faster than an HDD.
c: Read the situation
Identify who will use the device and what they need most.
Capacity and cost
High capacity may matter more than speed for a large archive; compare price per GB.
Speed and portability
A handheld device benefits from fast, light storage.
Durability and reliability
Consider knocks, long-term service and the need for backups; no medium is infallible.
Justification means linking
Do not just list 'fast'. Explain how that benefits the user in the question.

m.q: Choose storage for a travel photographer who edits large files daily.
st: Need: edit large image files frequently while travelling.
Choose a portable SSD.
Reason 1: fast transfer and file opening helps editing large files.
Reason 2: no moving parts reduces risk of impact damage while travelling.
Mention a limitation: SSDs can cost more per GB; keep a backup elsewhere.

w: Recommend a device for regularly carrying schoolwork between computers.
USB flash drive or portable SSD: portable, small, no moving parts.
Recommend a medium for archiving large amounts cheaply.
HDD: high capacity and often lower cost per GB.
Why is reliability different from storage capacity?
Reliability concerns how dependably data can be accessed or retained; capacity is amount stored.

k.q: Compare storage cost per gigabyte using variables.
p: Predict the result in pounds per GB.
Write one sentence linking cost per GB to a school’s archive requirement.
k.a: 0.06 pounds per GB (6p). At £45 it is £0.045 (4.5p) per GB. Lower cost per GB is useful when buying high-capacity school archives.

e: State two characteristics used when comparing secondary storage. [2]
Any two of capacity, speed, portability, durability, reliability, cost.
Justify a suitable device for a tablet that may be dropped. [3]
Solid-state device/SSD: no moving parts so more resistant to shocks; compact/portable; suitable for a mobile device.
A school has two drives: A is £40/400 GB and B £54/900 GB. Calculate cost per GB and identify the cheaper option. [3]
A = £0.10/GB. B = £0.06/GB. B has lower cost per GB.
v: Amount of data a storage device can hold.
Ability to withstand physical wear or impact.
Likelihood of operating correctly over time.
Device price divided by capacity in GB.
x: The fastest storage technology is always the best choice in every scenario.

o: Distinguish bits, nibbles, bytes and larger storage units.
Convert units using the conversion specified.
Calculate how much storage a set of files requires.
r: Recommend storage for a portable video editor who needs fast access. Give one reason.
Portable SSD: fast file access and good resistance to physical knocks.
Explain the difference between bitmap resolution and colour depth.
Resolution describes pixel dimensions; colour depth is bits per pixel.
Which technology does a conventional HDD use?
Magnetic storage.
Drive A costs £48 for 600 GB. Drive B costs £75 for 1,500 GB. Calculate the cost per GB of each and identify the cheaper option per GB.
A: £48 ÷ 600 = £0.08/GB. B: £75 ÷ 1,500 = £0.05/GB. B has the lower cost per GB.
c: Small units
1 bit is a binary digit; 1 nibble is 4 bits; 1 byte is 8 bits.
Larger units
KB, MB, GB, TB increase in size. OCR J277 commonly uses decimal multipliers where 1 KB = 1,000 bytes.
Conversion direction
Larger to smaller: multiply. Smaller to larger: divide.
File totals
Multiply number of files by the size of each file; use consistent units.
Exam accuracy
Always read the unit definition provided in the question and show conversion steps.

m.q: A class has 50 video clips of 8 MB each. Estimate the total in GB.
st: Multiply files by size: 50 × 8 MB = 400 MB.
Use the stated decimal convention, 1,000 MB = 1 GB.
Check: the result is smaller than 1 GB, which makes sense.
State the answer with units: 0.4 GB.

w: Convert 40 bytes to bits.
Convert 9,000 KB to MB using 1,000 KB per MB.
9 MB.
A 2 GB drive stores 200 MB videos. How many fit?
2,000 ÷ 200 = 10 videos, using the decimal convention.

k.q: Turn a bits-to-bytes calculation into OCR ERL code.
p: Write code to store 5 file sizes of 200 MB and print the total.
k.a: 30 bytes; for 400 bits gives 50 bytes. Example: fileSize = 200; count = 5; print(fileSize * count) displays 1,000 MB.

e: Convert 7 bytes into bits. [2]
Convert 3.5 GB into MB when 1 GB = 1,000 MB. [2]
A laptop contains 24 files of 125 MB each. Calculate the total in GB using decimal units. [3]
v: A storage unit; in decimal conversion, 1 GB = 1,000 MB.
x: When converting from bytes into bits, multiply by 8.

016.t: The CPU: ALU, CU and Cache
o: Explain the purpose of the CPU.
Identify ALU, CU and cache responsibilities.
Connect CPU components to executing instructions.
r: Convert 2.5 GB into MB using 1 GB = 1,000 MB.
Explain why lossless compression is essential for program source code.
It allows the exact original instructions to be reconstructed.
Why can frequent virtual-memory swapping slow a computer?
Access to secondary storage is slower than access to RAM.
An uncompressed 128 × 64 bitmap uses eight bits per pixel. Calculate its raw size in bytes and decimal KB.
c: CPU is the processor
It executes program instructions and processes data. It coordinates operations with memory and devices.
Control Unit (CU)
Controls and coordinates the fetch–decode–execute process; sends control signals.
Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU)
Performs arithmetic calculations and logical/comparison operations.
Cache
Small, fast memory close to/in the CPU that stores frequently used instructions/data.
Working together
A CPU fetches instructions, decodes what to do, and executes with help from its components.

m.q: Describe how the CPU handles an instruction to add two numbers.
st: The next instruction is fetched from memory.
The control unit decodes the instruction to identify the operation and operands.
Required numerical values are made available to the CPU.
The ALU performs the addition.
The result can be held in a register such as the accumulator and used by the program.

w: Which part handles adding two values?
ALU.
Which part coordinates the operation?
Control Unit (CU).
Why is cache typically smaller than main RAM?
It is faster and more costly per unit of storage, so the CPU keeps a small amount of frequently needed data there.

k.q: Use two assignments and an addition to model processing.
p: Change b to 9 and calculate again.
Write a version using a variable called total for the result.
k.a: 12, then 14 when b = 9; total = a + b; print(total). The ALU conceptually performs arithmetic; the code is not hardware emulation.

e: State the purpose of the CPU. [2]
Processes data and executes instructions in a computer system.
Describe one function of the CU and one of the ALU. [4]
CU coordinates/decodes and directs operations; ALU carries out arithmetic and logical operations.
Explain how cache can improve performance. [2]
Stores frequently used data/instructions near the CPU, reducing the need for slower RAM access.
v: Central processing unit: executes program instructions.
Arithmetic logic unit: performs calculations and logical operations.
Control unit: coordinates and decodes CPU instructions.
Fast local memory storing frequently used information.
x: The ALU is responsible for storing every document permanently.

o: Explain the order of the fetch–decode–execute cycle.
State roles of PC, MAR, MDR and accumulator.
Trace how instructions and data move through the CPU.
r: What is the difference between the Control Unit (CU) and Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU)?
The CU decodes/co-ordinates instructions; the ALU performs arithmetic and logical operations.
Perform a two-place logical right shift on 10010110.
What does sound bit depth measure, and how does increasing it affect raw file size?
Bits used per sample; increasing bit depth increases the raw file size at the same sample rate and duration.
A CPU repeatedly adds two numbers. Explain the roles of the CU, ALU and cache in completing this task efficiently.
CU co-ordinates/decodes instructions; ALU performs each addition; cache provides fast access to frequently used data or instructions, reducing slower RAM accesses.
c: Program Counter (PC)
Stores the address of the next instruction to fetch.
Memory Address Register (MAR)
Holds the address of a memory location being accessed.
Memory Data Register (MDR)
Holds data or an instruction transferred to/from main memory.
Accumulator (ACC)
Holds results of calculations performed by the ALU.
The cycle
Fetch instruction from RAM, decode it in the CU, execute it; then repeat. The PC advances unless a jump changes it.

m.q: Walk through a simple CPU instruction from start to finish.
st: FETCH: The PC holds the address of the next instruction.
Copy that address to MAR; the address is sent to memory.
Read the instruction from memory into MDR; PC typically advances.
DECODE: CU interprets the instruction and prepares signals.
EXECUTE: ALU/CU performs the operation; if it calculates a value, ACC may hold the result.

w: Which register holds the next instruction's address?
PC.
Which register receives data/instructions read from memory?
MDR.
Which register can store an ALU calculation result?
Accumulator (ACC).

k.q: Write instructions in sequence to model the cycle.
p: Predict the three output lines in order.
Change the code to display the cycle twice.
Explain why three print instructions show only an illustration of the FDE cycle.
k.a: FETCH, DECODE, EXECUTE in order. Repeat the three lines or use an appropriate loop once taught. The print statements only label stages, not carry out hardware operations.

e: State what PC and MAR each store. [2]
PC: address of next instruction. MAR: address of location being accessed.
Explain the role of MDR in fetching an instruction. [2]
It receives the instruction/data transferred from memory and holds it for the CPU.
Describe the fetch–decode–execute cycle. [4]
PC identifies instruction address; address moved to MAR and instruction fetched into MDR; CU decodes; CPU/ALU executes; cycle repeats.
v: Program Counter: address of next instruction.
Memory Address Register: address currently accessed.
Memory Data Register: data/instruction being transferred.
x: The MDR stores the address of the next instruction.

o: Retrieve and apply Autumn 1 knowledge across systems and data.
Explain answers using precise OCR J277 terminology.
Identify personal gaps and next steps.
r: What do the Program Counter (PC) and Memory Data Register (MDR) each store?
PC: address of the next instruction. MDR: data or an instruction being transferred to/from memory.
Convert hexadecimal 3A into denary.
What is virtual memory, and why can it reduce performance?
Secondary storage used when RAM is insufficient; swapping to slower storage can reduce performance.
A 200 × 100 bitmap uses four-bit colour depth. Calculate its raw pixel-data size in bits, bytes and decimal KB. Suggest one way to reduce the file size without changing the pixel dimensions.
200 × 100 × 4 = 80,000 bits = 10,000 bytes = 10 KB. Reduce colour depth or use compression, if appropriate.
c: Exam command words
State = give a fact; describe = give features/steps; explain = give a reason or cause; justify = link choice to context.
Show calculations
Formula → numbers → result → units. A calculator is not allowed on J277/01.
Link marks to points
A 3-mark explanation usually needs more than one distinct linked idea.
Mixed questions
Switch confidently between data representation, memory and CPU architecture.
Review
Mark against worked criteria, correct one misunderstanding and identify one topic to revisit.

m.q: Model a mixed, 4-mark GCSE-style answer about image file size and storage choice.
st: For a 100 × 50 bitmap at 4 bits per pixel, write width × height × depth.
For a portable device, propose an SSD and explain: no moving parts makes it more resistant to knocks.
State each unit and make the contextual justification clear.

w: A text document must remain exact: lossy or lossless?
Lossless because all original data must be restored.
What are the three main FDE stages?
Fetch, decode, execute.
Name the CPU component for arithmetic and the memory used for active programs.
ALU and RAM.

k.q: On your mini-whiteboard, write a short OCR ERL program combining arithmetic and output.
k.code:
width = 20
height = 10
depth = 4
print(width * height * depth)
p: Predict the raw bitmap size in bits.
Change depth to 8 and predict the new size.
Add a second line to print the number of bytes.
k.a: 800 bits, then 1,600 bits at eight-bit depth. print(width * height * depth DIV 8) shows 200 bytes after the change.

e: Perform an 8-bit left shift of 00110001 by one place. [2]
Explain why an SSD might suit a laptop better than an HDD. [3]
No moving parts makes it less vulnerable to movement/knocks; faster access is useful for loading programs; often compact/light.
A 50 × 40 image uses 8 bits per pixel. Calculate raw data size in bytes. [3]
Describe two distinct roles of PC and MDR in fetching instructions. [4]
PC gives next instruction address; MDR holds the instruction/data retrieved from memory. Explain their roles in fetch.
v: Retrieving the next instruction from main memory.
Reducing file size for storage or transmission.
Bits used to encode each pixel.
Memory loses its data when power is removed.
x: The Program Counter holds the address of the next instruction.
